title: Repeat winners where entrants are known
question: Where a drawing or queue publishes both who entered and who won, did the same entrants win more often than their entries would explain?
finding: Only one drawing on disk publishes entrants and winners for more than one year: the condominium-conversion lottery of 2001 to 2013. There the same buildings did not keep winning: 804 of 1,996 buildings won once, 7 are marked winners twice and 1,185 never won. What stands out is the reverse: a first entry won 3.3% of the time and a building on its 8th entry 71.6%. The longer a building had been entering, the better its chance; that is what the code prescribes, since Subdivision Code section 1396.3 gives a building one extra ticket for every lottery it lost, with no cap. Even with tickets weighted that way, about 85 first entries would have been expected to win and 54 did, and about 118 sixth-or-later entries against 237: the remaining gap is in the direction expected from the separate Pool A, which converts buildings that lost three or more times ahead of the ticket draw. The State’s 2026 neighborhood liquor-licence drawing had 8 entrants for 5 licences and is the only year online, so no entrant can be seen winning twice. The taxi medallion list was a queue, not a draw.
how: Condominium lottery: every building (block and lot) is followed through the 13 yearly result files. The yearly chance is winners divided by entries. "By the code’s ticket rule" gives each entry one ticket plus one per earlier loss on disk and shares the year’s winners out by tickets; "the same chance" gives each entry its year’s chance. Each comparison adds the chances up and uses the normal approximation to that sum. In the all-years row, first-try and long-wait figures use only buildings first seen after 2001, because the first file hides earlier entries; in the yearly rows the long-wait figure counts every building on at least its sixth entry on disk. Liquor licences: entrants and ranks from the State’s 2026 result file; the number of licences from the State’s announcement. Taxi: one row per offer letter; a driver is one list number.
limits: The rule is read from the code text in the site’s “What the codes require” page: section 1396.3, which prevails over the original section 1396.1, gives each building in Pool B “plus one lottery ticket for every lottery in which the building participated but failed to be selected for conversion”, and sets apart a Pool A of up to 100 units for buildings that lost three or more lotteries, ranked by how often they lost. Tickets are earned by losing, not by years of owner occupancy; occupancy decides only whether a building may enter. Section 1396.3 was added by an ordinance approved 2 February 2007; the original 1396.1 also counted losses but capped them (“No building in Pool B shall receive more than five tickets.”). The ticket-weighted test counts only losses on disk, leaves out Pool A and unit counts, and so understates the advantage of long waiters. A building chosen but not converted is not counted as having lost (1396.3(f)), which is one innocent reason for a building to be marked a winner twice. The result files list buildings, not owners: one owner with several buildings would not show here (the aliases analysis tests that by address). A building marked a winner twice may have dropped out after the first win. The liquor drawing can be tested for one year only. Scored rounds, where entrants and winners are also known, are in their own tables because chance is the wrong yardstick for them. The aliases analysis (the site’s “One owner behind several names” page, "Drawings, licence lists and grant rounds") holds the test for one owner at several lottery buildings; it is not repeated here.

columns.t: Sixth or later entry that won

rows.against: By the code’s ticket rule (one extra ticket per lottery lost), about 85 first-time entries would have won; 54 did (about 1 in 2,400). About 118 entries on the sixth or later try would have won; 237 did (less than one in a million). If every entry had had the same chance, which is not the rule, the expectations would be 201 and 67.
rows.note: Entrants are buildings, shown as counts only. 14 buildings entered again after a year in which they are marked a winner, and 7 are marked a winner twice. 1,185 buildings never won, 591 of them still in the last drawing.

rows.drawing: State liquor-licence priority drawing, neighborhood-restricted licences (State Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control)
rows.against: Each of the 8 entrants had the same 62.5% chance of one of 5 licences. With one round on disk no entrant can have won twice.
rows.note: The State publishes only the current year’s list and replaces it each cycle, so repeat entrants and repeat winners across 2019–2025 cannot be counted.

rows.drawing: State special-legislation liquor licences, hospitality zone (State Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control)
rows.against: No drawing was needed: 9 applicants for 10 licences.
rows.note: The published list is in alphabetical order, not a ranking. One of the applicants applied in a personal name and is not shown.

rows.drawing: Taxi medallion waiting list: offers in list order (Municipal Transportation Agency)
rows.against: A queue, not a draw: chance does not apply. An offer is not a medallion; drivers could decline or fail to qualify and be offered again.
rows.note: 582 offer letters in 23 notices went to 514 list numbers; 65 list numbers were offered more than once, none more than 3 times. Drivers are counted by list number and never named. The list held 3,029 people when it was closed to new names (2012 report).

rows.drawing: Taxi Medallion Sales Pilot Program: participating buyers and sellers (Municipal Transportation Agency)
rows.against: Buyers were offered medallions in list order; no list of completed sales by buyer is published.
rows.note: 230 participating buyers by list number and 168 participating sellers by medallion number; 0 of the buyers’ list numbers also appear in the 2009–2013 offer notices.
